details:
**Battle of Waterloo**
Napoleon's final defeat in 1815, in present-day Belgium, at the hands of the Seventh Coalition led by the British Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Gebhard von Blücher, whose late arrival decided the battle. It is the most common giveaway in questions about him.

**Exiles to Elba and St. Helena**
After losing the War of the Sixth Coalition in 1814, Napoleon abdicated and was exiled to the Mediterranean island of Elba. He escaped and briefly retook power in the Hundred Days, and after Waterloo he was exiled to the remote South Atlantic island of St. Helena, where he died in 1821.

**Battle of Austerlitz**
Napoleon's greatest victory, in 1805, over the Austrian and Russian armies of the Third Coalition. He deliberately gave up the high ground of the Pratzen Heights to lure the allies into attacking, then struck their weakened center; the Treaty of Pressburg then took large territories from Austria.

**Peninsular War and Joseph Bonaparte**
The war in Spain and Portugal that began after Napoleon placed his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne in 1808. The Dos de Mayo uprising in Madrid, French defeats at Bailén and Salamanca, the British Lines of Torres Vedras that stopped Marshal André Masséna, and Arthur Wellesley (later Wellington) all wore down French forces; Spanish resistance gave rise to the term "guerrilla" and to the liberal Constitution of Cádiz.

**Invasion of Russia (1812)**
Napoleon's disastrous campaign against Tsar Alexander I after the collapse of the Treaty of Tilsit. He won the bloody Battle of Borodino against Mikhail Kutuzov and entered Moscow, which the Russians burned; the winter retreat, including the crossing of the Berezina River, destroyed most of the Grande Armée, a loss famously charted in Charles Minard's flow map.

**Coup of 18 Brumaire**
The 1799 coup in which Napoleon overthrew the Directory and made himself First Consul of France. Karl Marx's essay "The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Napoleon" compares it to the 1851 coup of Napoleon's nephew Napoleon III, saying history repeats "first as tragedy, then as farce."

**Napoleonic Code**
The Civil Code of 1804 that Napoleon enacted as First Consul, unifying French law and replacing the patchwork of customary law in the north and Roman law in the south. It remains the basis of the legal systems of France, Belgium, Luxembourg, and many other countries.

**Concordat of 1801**
Napoleon's agreement with Pope Pius VII that restored the Catholic Church's status in France while keeping the state's control over the clergy. Pius VII was present at Napoleon's 1804 coronation in Notre-Dame Cathedral, where Napoleon crowned himself emperor.

**"Whiff of grapeshot"**
Thomas Carlyle's phrase for Napoleon's use of cannon fire to disperse a royalist uprising in Paris in 1795 (13 Vendémiaire). Earlier, in 1793, he had made his name by helping recapture the port of Toulon from royalist and British forces.

**Continental System**
Napoleon's economic blockade of Great Britain, established by the Berlin Decree (1806) and Milan Decree (1807), which banned trade with Britain throughout his empire and allied states. Britain responded with its Orders in Council.

**Battle of Jena-Auerstedt**
Twin 1806 battles in which Napoleon crushed the army of Prussia's Frederick William III. At Auerstedt, Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout defeated a Prussian force about twice his size, prompting Napoleon to quip that the marshal was "seeing double."

**Josephine and Marie Louise**
Napoleon's first wife was Josephine de Beauharnais, whom he divorced because she had not produced an heir. He then married Marie Louise of Austria, remarking that he had "married a womb"; she gave birth to his son and later became Duchess of Parma.

**Treaty of Campo Formio**
The 1797 treaty with Austria that ended Napoleon's first Italian campaign, in which he had won battles such as Castiglione during the Siege of Mantua. It partitioned the Republic of Venice, giving Venice itself to Austria.

**Battle of Marengo**
Napoleon's 1800 victory over Austria in northern Italy after he crossed the Alps, which secured his position as First Consul. He named his favorite horse Marengo after it.

**Corsican origins**
Napoleon was born on Corsica in 1769 and began his career as an artillery officer in the La Fère regiment. A falling-out with the Corsican nationalist Pasquale Paoli forced his family to flee the island in 1793.
